title: English: a global language
subtitle: lexicon, loanword, borrowing, false friend
summary: Talk about where English words come from - the lexicon, word stock, loanwords and borrowings - and spot the false friends that look familiar but mean something else.

lesson.heading: A language that welcomes words
lesson.text: Some languages do not easily accept words from other languages into their **lexicon** - the specialist term for a language's vocabulary. English has always welcomed them. It is estimated that English vocabulary has its **sources** in at least 120 languages. English started out with a basic Anglo-Saxon **word stock**, that is, its basic set of words.

examples.text: A linguist may talk about a language's vocabulary as its **lexicon**.
English began with a small Anglo-Saxon **word stock** and grew from there.
Where a word originates from is called its **source**.

lesson.note: Anglo-Saxon is another name for Old English.

lesson.heading: Invaders and scholars
lesson.text: **Viking** invaders (Norse, from the north of Europe) and **Norman** invaders (from Normandy in northern France) from the 9th century onwards **enriched** the language enormously - they made it richer. Both sets of invaders had an enormous **impact on** English, which explains why English often seems to have several words for the same basic **concept**, or idea.

examples.text: The Vikings brought new words of Germanic origin; the Normans spoke a form of French.
The invasions had a huge **impact on** the language.

lesson.heading: Loanwords and borrowings
lesson.text: During the Renaissance of the 15th to the 17th centuries, scholars introduced many words of **classical origin** - from Latin or Ancient Greek. And English speakers' contact with the world as explorers, traders and holiday-makers has had linguistic **consequences**: results affecting language. Words taken from other languages are called **loanwords** or **borrowings**.

examples.text: Ancient Greek and Latin are referred to as **classical** languages.
A loanword can also be termed a **borrowing**.
A **consequence** is something that happens as a result of something else.

lesson.heading: English words from other languages
rows: yellowy-orange substance from tree resin, used in jewellery
list of people's turns for jobs
an amusing or unusual way of attracting attention
medicine to make you feel stronger and better
child's bed with high vertical sides
entertainment where ordinary people sing to popular music
net hung up and used as a bed
men's headwear made from a long piece of cloth

lesson.heading: False friends
lesson.text: Some English words may look like words in your own language but have a different meaning. Such words are known as **false friends**. The German word *Gift* looks like the English word **gift**, which means present, but in German it actually means poison.

examples.text: English **sympathetic** resembles a word meaning simply *nice* in many European languages, but in English it means understanding and caring about someone else's suffering.
A Spanish speaker may read **complexion** as physical build; in English it is the appearance of the skin on a person's face.
**Destitute** looks like Spanish *destituido* (removed from a job) but means without money, food, home or possessions.

lesson.note: The pronunciation of a borrowed word in English may be quite different from its pronunciation in the language it came from.

lesson.heading: English words that have travelled outwards
rows: parliament, Tory, boycott, budget, inflation, strike
car ferry, container, freight, computer chip, cable TV
lesson.note: These words may not all have originated in English. Pudding comes from an old French word, but it seems to have moved into other languages from English.

lesson.text: Loanword and borrowing mean exactly the same thing - a word taken from another language - so you can use either.

exercises.prompt: A linguist may talk about a language's vocabulary as its ___.
exercises.explanation: Lexicon is the specialist term for the set of words a language has.

exercises.prompt: Old English is also known as ___.
exercises.explanation: Anglo-Saxon is another name for Old English, the basic word stock of English.

exercises.prompt: Ancient Greek and Latin are referred to as ___ languages.
exercises.hint: (Renaissance scholars introduced words of this origin)
exercises.explanation: Words of classical origin come from Latin or Ancient Greek.

exercises.prompt: A loanword can also be termed a ___.
exercises.explanation: Loanword and borrowing both mean a word taken from another language.

exercises.prompt: Where something originates from can be called its ___.
exercises.explanation: A source is where something comes from.

exercises.prompt: A word for something that happens as a result of something else is a ___.
exercises.hint: (contact with the world had linguistic ones)
exercises.explanation: A consequence is a result of something else.

exercises.prompt: A synonym for effect or influence is ___.
exercises.hint: (the invaders had an enormous ... on English)
exercises.explanation: The Vikings and Normans had an enormous impact on English vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: The opposite of impoverish or make poorer is ___.
exercises.hint: (the invaders did this to the language)
exercises.explanation: To enrich something is to make it richer.

exercises.prompt: Match each loanword with the language it came into English from.
We're having a ___ evening at school tonight - it should be great fun.
exercises.explanation: Karaoke, from Japanese, is entertainment where people sing to recorded popular music.

exercises.prompt: Most babies these days have an injection to protect them from getting ___.
exercises.explanation: Mumps is a childhood illness; we say have mumps.

exercises.prompt: I have some lovely ___ earrings. They match my orange scarf perfectly.
exercises.explanation: Amber is a yellowy-orange substance originating from tree resin and used in jewellery.

exercises.prompt: Have a refreshing drink of lemon and honey every morning - it'll be just the ___ you need to feel better again.
exercises.explanation: A tonic is a medicine or drink that makes you feel stronger and better.

exercises.prompt: Who's on the ___ for the cleaning this week?
exercises.explanation: A roster is a list of people's turns for jobs.

exercises.prompt: The clowns went out into the street as a ___ to advertise their circus.
exercises.explanation: A gimmick, from German, is an amusing or unusual way of attracting attention.

exercises.statement: The German word Gift is a false friend, because it means poison and not present.
exercises.explanation: Correct - false friends look like words in your own language but mean something different.

exercises.statement: In English, sympathetic simply means nice.
exercises.explanation: In English sympathetic has a much narrower meaning: understanding and caring about someone else's suffering.

exercises.prompt: Sort these English source words that have travelled into other languages.
Put this sentence about English vocabulary in order.
exercises.answer: English has always welcomed words from other languages
exercises.explanation: Unlike some languages, English readily accepts loanwords into its lexicon.
